title: The awkward arithmetic of tipping
text: {{1}} the United States, waiting tables is paid for through tips, and the expectation of twenty per cent is so entrenched {{2}} refusing to tip is widely read as an insult. Servers, {{3}} base wages are set on the assumption of tips, depend on the custom for {{4}} actual income. The habit {{5}} spread far beyond its origins, and customs differ wildly from one country to the next: {{6}} counts as generous in New York may seem excessive in Tokyo, {{7}} a tip can feel awkward or even rude. Economists still argue {{8}} the whole institution — wages subsidised by voluntary guilt — makes any sense at all, yet the dinner bill keeps arriving with a blank line at the bottom.

gaps.hint: conjunction: so entrenched ___ refusing is read
relative: servers, ___ base wages are set
gaps.explanation: 'Whose' links the servers to their wages.
The income belongs to the servers: their income.
Present perfect with a singular subject: has spread.

gaps.hint: relative adverb: in Tokyo, ___ a tip can feel rude
gaps.explanation: 'Where' refers back to Tokyo as the place.

gaps.hint: conjunction: argue ___ the institution makes sense
gaps.explanation: An indirect yes/no question after 'argue': whether.
